modules.title: 8.1 General Properties of the Non-Metals
modules.html:
The non-metals occupy the upper right-hand block of the periodic table (together with hydrogen, which sits apart on the left). They are the elements whose atoms have four or more electrons in the outermost shell and therefore gain or share electrons rather than lose them. Fourteen of the 118 known elements are non-metals; six more (B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te) are metalloids with intermediate behaviour.

Physical properties of non-metals

  • State: gases (\(H_2, N_2, O_2, F_2, Cl_2\), the noble gases), one liquid (\(Br_2\)) and solids (C, S, P, I, Se).
  • Appearance: dull, not lustrous (iodine and graphite are exceptions).
  • Malleability: solid non-metals are brittle — they shatter when struck because there is no sea of mobile electrons to allow layers to slide.
  • Conductivity: poor conductors of heat and electricity (graphite conducts along its layers; silicon and germanium are semiconductors).
  • Density and melting point: generally low, because the molecules are held by weak van der Waals forces. Giant covalent non-metals (diamond, graphite, silicon) are the striking exceptions with extremely high melting points.
  • Electronegativity: high — fluorine (4.0) is the most electronegative element known.

Chemical properties

  1. With oxygen: they form acidic oxides (or neutral oxides). \(S + O_2 \rightarrow SO_2\); \(SO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow H_2SO_3\). \(CO\), \(NO\) and \(N_2O\) are neutral oxides.
  2. With hydrogen: they form covalent hydrides, many of which are acidic in water: \(HCl, H_2S, HBr\). \(NH_3\) is the notable basic hydride.
  3. With metals: they form ionic salts by accepting electrons: \(2Na + Cl_2 \rightarrow 2NaCl\).
  4. As oxidising agents: the halogens and oxygen readily accept electrons, e.g. \(Cl_2 + 2e^- \rightarrow 2Cl^-\).

Occurrence and extraction in outline

Nitrogen and oxygen are obtained by the fractional distillation of liquefied air (nitrogen boils off first at \(-196^{\circ}C\), then argon at \(-186^{\circ}C\), then oxygen at \(-183^{\circ}C\)). Carbon occurs free as diamond, graphite and coal; sulphur occurs free in volcanic deposits and is mined by the Frasch process. Halogens never occur free because they are too reactive; chlorine is obtained industrially from brine by electrolysis.

Why the distinction matters in the examination

Whenever a question asks whether an oxide is acidic, basic or amphoteric, first classify the element. Metal oxide → basic (\(Na_2O, CaO\)); non-metal oxide → acidic (\(CO_2, SO_3, P_4O_{10}\)); a few oxides of metals near the metal/non-metal boundary (\(Al_2O_3, ZnO, PbO\)) are amphoteric; \(CO, NO, N_2O, H_2O\) are neutral. This single rule earns marks in almost every WAEC/NECO paper.
examples: Classify each oxide as acidic, basic, amphoteric or neutral: SO3, CaO, ZnO, N2O.
Explain why solid non-metals are brittle while metals are malleable.

modules.title: 8.2 Carbon and its Allotropes
modules.html:
Carbon is unique: no other element forms so many compounds (over ten million) because its atoms catenate — they bond covalently to one another in chains, branches and rings — and it forms strong multiple bonds. Carbon exists in several allotropes: different forms of the same element in the same physical state.

Diamond

Each carbon atom is \(sp^3\) hybridised and bonded tetrahedrally to four others (bond angle \(109.5^{\circ}\)) in a giant covalent lattice. Consequences:

  • Hardest natural substance — used in glass cutters, drilling bits and abrasives.
  • Very high melting point (about \(3550^{\circ}C\)) — millions of strong covalent bonds must be broken.
  • Non-conductor of electricity — all four valence electrons are localised in bonds.
  • High refractive index and dispersion — hence its use as a gemstone.
  • Density about \(3.5\ g\,cm^{-3}\), higher than graphite because the packing is compact.

Graphite

Each atom is \(sp^2\) hybridised and bonded to only three others in flat hexagonal layers (bond angle \(120^{\circ}\)). The fourth electron is delocalised between the layers, and the layers themselves are held by weak van der Waals forces. Consequences:

  • Conducts electricity — used for electrodes in electrolysis and in dry cells.
  • Soft and slippery — layers slide over one another; used as a lubricant and in pencil "lead".
  • Lower density (\(2.2\ g\,cm^{-3}\)) than diamond because of the wide gaps between layers.
  • Also has a very high melting point, since melting still requires covalent bonds within layers to break.

Amorphous (non-crystalline) carbon

Charcoal, coke, lampblack, animal charcoal and carbon black are microcrystalline graphite with very large surface areas. Wood charcoal and animal charcoal are used as adsorbents to decolourise brown sugar solution and to purify liquids; activated charcoal is used in gas masks and water filters. Coke is the reducing agent in the blast furnace; lampblack is used in printer's ink, boot polish and as a filler in tyres.

Newer allotropes

Fullerenes (e.g. buckminsterfullerene, \(C_{60}\)) are closed cages of 60 atoms shaped like a football; nanotubes are rolled graphite sheets with enormous tensile strength; graphene is a single graphite layer.

Chemical properties of carbon

  • Burns in excess air: \(C + O_2 \rightarrow CO_2\); in limited air: \(2C + O_2 \rightarrow 2CO\).
  • Reduces metal oxides: \(2CuO + C \rightarrow 2Cu + CO_2\); \(ZnO + C \rightarrow Zn + CO\).
  • Reduces hot concentrated acids: \(C + 4HNO_3 \rightarrow CO_2 + 4NO_2 + 2H_2O\); \(C + 2H_2SO_4 \rightarrow CO_2 + 2SO_2 + 2H_2O\).
  • With steam at high temperature gives water gas: \(C + H_2O \rightarrow CO + H_2\).
examples: Compare the structure and electrical conductivity of diamond and graphite.
Write the equation for the reduction of copper(II) oxide by carbon.

modules.title: 8.3 Oxides of Carbon and Trioxocarbonates
modules.html:
Carbon forms two important oxides — carbon(II) oxide (carbon monoxide) and carbon(IV) oxide (carbon dioxide). They differ sharply in preparation, properties and hazard.

Carbon(IV) oxide, \(CO_2\)

Laboratory preparation: dilute hydrochloric acid on marble chips in a flat-bottomed flask, gas collected by downward delivery (upward displacement of air) because it is denser than air:

\(CaCO_3 + 2HCl \rightarrow CaCl_2 + H_2O + CO_2\)

Dilute \(H_2SO_4\) is not used because insoluble \(CaSO_4\) coats the marble and stops the reaction.

Properties: colourless, odourless gas, about 1.5 times denser than air, slightly soluble in water forming weak trioxocarbonate(IV) acid \(H_2CO_3\); does not burn and does not support combustion (except for burning magnesium: \(2Mg + CO_2 \rightarrow 2MgO + C\)). It turns lime water milky: \(Ca(OH)_2 + CO_2 \rightarrow CaCO_3 + H_2O\); with excess \(CO_2\) the milkiness disappears as soluble \(Ca(HCO_3)_2\) forms.

Uses: fire extinguishers (it is dense and non-supporter of combustion), fizzy drinks, baking powder, solid \(CO_2\) ("dry ice") as a refrigerant, and as the raw material of photosynthesis.

Carbon(II) oxide, \(CO\)

Preparation: dehydration of methanoic acid with concentrated \(H_2SO_4\), \(HCOOH \xrightarrow{conc.H_2SO_4} CO + H_2O\); or by passing \(CO_2\) over red-hot coke, \(CO_2 + C \rightarrow 2CO\).

Properties: colourless, odourless, neutral oxide, almost insoluble in water, burns with a blue flame (\(2CO + O_2 \rightarrow 2CO_2\)) and is a powerful reducing agent: \(Fe_2O_3 + 3CO \rightarrow 2Fe + 3CO_2\) in the blast furnace.

Toxicity: \(CO\) binds to haemoglobin about 250 times more strongly than oxygen, forming stable carboxyhaemoglobin, so the blood can no longer carry oxygen. It is produced by faulty generators, charcoal stoves and car exhausts in poorly ventilated rooms — the classic cause of "generator deaths".

Trioxocarbonate(IV) salts

These are salts of the weak acid \(H_2CO_3\); the normal salts contain \(CO_3^{2-}\) and the acid salts contain \(HCO_3^{-}\).

  • Solubility: only the trioxocarbonates of \(Na^+\), \(K^+\) and \(NH_4^+\) are soluble; all others are insoluble.
  • Action of heat: all trioxocarbonates except those of sodium and potassium decompose: \(CaCO_3 \rightarrow CaO + CO_2\); \(2Cu(NO_3)\)-type patterns should not be confused — for copper, \(CuCO_3 \rightarrow CuO + CO_2\) (green to black). All hydrogentrioxocarbonates decompose on heating, even \(NaHCO_3\): \(2NaHCO_3 \rightarrow Na_2CO_3 + H_2O + CO_2\), the reaction that makes bread and cake rise.
  • With dilute acid: every trioxocarbonate effervesces, giving \(CO_2\): \(Na_2CO_3 + 2HCl \rightarrow 2NaCl + H_2O + CO_2\). This is the standard test for the carbonate ion when combined with the lime-water test.

Uses: \(Na_2CO_3\) (washing soda) softens water and makes glass; \(NaHCO_3\) (baking soda) is used in baking, in antacids and in fire extinguishers; \(CaCO_3\) is used to make cement, quicklime and as a blast-furnace flux.
examples: Describe with an equation the laboratory preparation of carbon(IV) oxide.
Explain why CO is far more dangerous than CO2 in a closed room.

modules.title: 8.4 Tests, Calculations and Laboratory Practice
modules.html:
This module gathers the practical, calculation and examination skills for the non-metal chemistry of carbon.

Identifying an unknown gas

GasTestObservation
\(CO_2\)Bubble into lime waterMilky; clears with excess gas
\(CO\)Apply a lighted splintBurns with a blue flame; product turns lime water milky
\(O_2\)Glowing splintRelights
\(H_2\)Lighted splintBurns with a "pop"
\(SO_2\)Acidified \(KMnO_4\) paperPurple decolourised; choking smell
\(NH_3\)Damp red litmusTurns blue; white fumes with \(HCl\)

Worked calculation 1 — mass to volume

What volume of \(CO_2\) at s.t.p. is produced when 25.0 g of calcium trioxocarbonate(IV) is completely decomposed? (\(Ca=40, C=12, O=16\); molar volume \(=22.4\ dm^3\)).

\(CaCO_3 \rightarrow CaO + CO_2\). Molar mass of \(CaCO_3 = 40+12+48 = 100\ g\,mol^{-1}\).

Moles \(= 25.0/100 = 0.25\ mol\). The mole ratio is 1:1, so \(n(CO_2)=0.25\ mol\).

Volume \(= 0.25 \times 22.4 = \mathbf{5.6\ dm^3}\).

Worked calculation 2 — percentage purity

10.0 g of impure limestone is heated strongly and gives 1.68 dm3 of \(CO_2\) at s.t.p. Find the percentage purity of the limestone.

\(n(CO_2) = 1.68/22.4 = 0.075\ mol\). From \(CaCO_3 \rightarrow CaO + CO_2\) the ratio is 1:1, so \(n(CaCO_3)=0.075\ mol\).

Mass of pure \(CaCO_3 = 0.075 \times 100 = 7.5\ g\).

Percentage purity \(= (7.5/10.0)\times 100 = \mathbf{75\%}\). Always check that the calculated mass of pure substance is smaller than the sample mass; this quick self-check catches arithmetic slips in the examination.

Worked calculation 3 — reducing power of \(CO\)

How many grams of iron are obtained when 320 g of \(Fe_2O_3\) is completely reduced by \(CO\)? (\(Fe=56, O=16\)).

\(Fe_2O_3 + 3CO \rightarrow 2Fe + 3CO_2\). \(M(Fe_2O_3)=160\), so \(n = 320/160 = 2\ mol\); \(n(Fe)=4\ mol\); \(m = 4\times56 = \mathbf{224\ g}\).

Practical safety and technique

  • Never heat a closed system: expanding gas can shatter the apparatus.
  • Remove the delivery tube from the water before removing the flame, otherwise "suck-back" cracks the hot test tube.
  • Generate and burn \(CO\) only in a fume cupboard — it has no smell to warn you.
  • Dry \(CO_2\) with concentrated \(H_2SO_4\), never with quicklime or soda lime, which would absorb it.

Examination strategy

Structured questions on this topic almost always follow the same three-part shape: (a) draw or describe the laboratory preparation with a correct equation, (b) state two properties that explain the method of collection and drying, (c) do one mole calculation. Rehearse the equations until they are automatic and write state symbols — they carry marks.
examples: Calculate the mass of iron formed from 480 g of Fe2O3 reduced by CO.
State the test that distinguishes CO2 from SO2.

quiz.q: Which of the following elements is a non-metal that exists as a liquid at room temperature?
quiz.solution: Bromine is the only non-metal liquid at room temperature; mercury is a liquid metal.

quiz.q: Non-metallic oxides are generally
quiz.solution: Non-metal oxides such as CO2 and SO3 dissolve in water to form acids.

quiz.q: Which oxide is neutral?
quiz.solution: CO, NO and N2O are neutral oxides; they form no acid with water.

quiz.q: The most electronegative element is
quiz.solution: Fluorine has an electronegativity of 4.0, the highest of all elements.

quiz.q: Diamond is hard because
options: each carbon is tetrahedrally bonded to four others in a giant lattice
its molecules are held by van der Waals forces
quiz.solution: Millions of strong covalent bonds in three dimensions make diamond extremely hard.

quiz.q: Graphite conducts electricity because
options: it has one delocalised electron per atom
quiz.solution: Only three of carbon's four valence electrons are used in bonding; the fourth is delocalised.

quiz.q: The bond angle in diamond is
quiz.solution: Diamond is sp3 hybridised, giving a tetrahedral 109.5 degree angle.

quiz.q: The bond angle within a graphite layer is
quiz.solution: sp2 hybridisation gives trigonal planar geometry with 120 degree angles.

quiz.q: Allotropes are
options: different elements with the same mass number
different forms of the same element in the same physical state
quiz.solution: Allotropy is the existence of an element in more than one form in the same state.

quiz.q: Graphite is used as a lubricant because
options: its layers slide over one another
quiz.solution: Weak van der Waals forces between layers allow easy sliding.

quiz.q: Which allotrope of carbon has the highest density?
quiz.solution: Diamond's compact tetrahedral packing gives about 3.5 g/cm3 against graphite's 2.2.

quiz.q: Animal charcoal is used to
quiz.solution: Charcoal adsorbs coloured impurities because of its large surface area.

quiz.q: Buckminsterfullerene has the formula
quiz.solution: C60 is the football-shaped fullerene named after Buckminster Fuller.

quiz.q: The laboratory preparation of carbon(IV) oxide uses
quiz.solution: Dilute H2SO4 forms insoluble CaSO4 which stops the reaction.

quiz.q: Carbon(IV) oxide is collected by
quiz.solution: CO2 is denser than air so it is collected by downward delivery.

quiz.q: Which gas turns lime water milky?
quiz.solution: CO2 forms insoluble CaCO3 with calcium hydroxide solution.

quiz.q: The milkiness formed when excess CO2 is passed through lime water disappears because
quiz.solution: Excess CO2 converts CaCO3 to soluble Ca(HCO3)2.

quiz.q: Burning magnesium continues to burn in CO2 because
quiz.solution: 2Mg + CO2 gives 2MgO + C, seen as a black deposit of carbon.

quiz.q: Solid carbon(IV) oxide is known as
quiz.solution: Solid CO2 sublimes without melting and is used as a refrigerant.

quiz.q: Carbon(II) oxide is poisonous because it
quiz.solution: CO binds haemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen does.

quiz.q: Carbon(II) oxide burns with a
quiz.solution: CO burns with a characteristic blue flame giving CO2.

quiz.q: In the blast furnace the chief reducing agent is
quiz.solution: Fe2O3 + 3CO gives 2Fe + 3CO2.

quiz.q: Water gas is a mixture of
quiz.solution: Steam passed over red-hot coke gives CO + H2.

quiz.q: Which trioxocarbonate is soluble in water?
quiz.solution: Only the trioxocarbonates of sodium, potassium and ammonium are soluble.

quiz.q: Which trioxocarbonate is NOT decomposed by heat?
quiz.solution: Sodium and potassium trioxocarbonates are stable to heat.

quiz.q: Heating sodium hydrogentrioxocarbonate gives
quiz.solution: 2NaHCO3 gives Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2, which raises dough in baking.

quiz.q: The gas evolved when dilute acid is added to a trioxocarbonate is
quiz.solution: All trioxocarbonates effervesce with acid to give CO2.

quiz.q: On heating, green copper(II) trioxocarbonate turns
quiz.solution: CuCO3 gives black CuO and CO2.

quiz.q: Washing soda is
quiz.solution: Hydrated sodium trioxocarbonate is washing soda.

quiz.q: Which is used to dry carbon(IV) oxide?
quiz.solution: Basic driers would absorb the acidic gas.

quiz.q: Non-metals are brittle because
options: there is no sea of mobile electrons allowing layers to slide
quiz.solution: Metallic bonding, absent in non-metals, permits deformation without fracture.

quiz.q: Nitrogen and oxygen are separated industrially by
quiz.solution: Liquid air is fractionally distilled; nitrogen boils off first.

quiz.q: Nitrogen boils at
quiz.solution: Nitrogen boils at -196 C, below argon and oxygen.

quiz.q: Sulphur is mined by the
quiz.solution: Superheated water melts underground sulphur, which is forced up by compressed air.

quiz.q: Which is a metalloid?
quiz.solution: Silicon shows both metallic and non-metallic behaviour and is a semiconductor.

quiz.q: Coke is used in the blast furnace mainly as
quiz.solution: Coke burns to give heat and CO, which reduces the ore.

quiz.q: Which reaction shows carbon acting as a reducing agent?
quiz.solution: Carbon removes oxygen from copper(II) oxide, reducing it to the metal.

quiz.q: 25 g of CaCO3 (M = 100) on full decomposition gives what volume of CO2 at s.t.p.?
How many moles of CO2 are in 4.4 g of the gas? (C=12, O=16)
The volume of CO2 produced by 0.5 mol of NaHCO3 on heating is
quiz.solution: 2NaHCO3 gives 1 CO2, so 0.25 mol x 22.4 = 5.6 dm3.

quiz.q: Lampblack is used in
quiz.solution: Lampblack is a fine amorphous carbon pigment.

quiz.q: Which statement about diamond and graphite is correct?
quiz.solution: They are both giant covalent, but only graphite conducts and is soft.

quiz.q: Concentrated tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid reacting with hot carbon gives
quiz.solution: C + 2H2SO4 gives CO2 + 2SO2 + 2H2O.

quiz.q: Which gas is neutral to litmus but burns?
quiz.solution: CO is a neutral oxide and a combustible gas.

quiz.q: Which non-metal is used in gas masks in activated form?
quiz.solution: Activated charcoal adsorbs toxic vapours.

quiz.q: The percentage purity of 10 g limestone yielding 1.68 dm3 CO2 at s.t.p. is
Which oxide is amphoteric?
quiz.solution: Aluminium oxide reacts with both acids and alkalis.

quiz.q: Carbon(IV) oxide extinguishes fire mainly because it
options: is denser than air and does not support combustion
quiz.solution: A dense blanket of CO2 cuts off the oxygen supply.

quiz.q: Which of these will NOT liberate CO2 from a trioxocarbonate?
quiz.solution: Alkalis do not displace CO2; only acids do.

quiz.q: Graphene is best described as
quiz.solution: Graphene is one atom-thick sheet of hexagonally bonded carbon.
